1. Core Clinical Tension: A 10-year-old child presents with drowsiness following a 4-day febrile illness, severe thrombocytopenia (35,000/μL), and normal-to-low blood pressure, with neuroimaging showing bilateral parieto-occipital white matter hyperintensities. The challenge is distinguishing acute viral encephalitis from posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) occurring in the absence of hypertension.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission presentation in a drowsy state with 4 days of fever, blood pressure 96/66 mm Hg, absence of rash/bleeding, and initial platelet count of 35,000/μL. Confirmatory testing begins with viral NS1 antigen testing and neuroimaging.
3. Differential Distinctions: Viral encephalitis was considered due to fever, drowsiness, and brain lesions, but ruled out by lack of diffusion restriction, absence of hemorrhage/contrast enhancement, and complete reversal on follow-up imaging. Classic hypertensive encephalopathy/PRES typically requires severe hypertension, whereas this child was normotensive/hypotensive, reflecting endothelial leakage driven by severe viral illness.
case_prompt: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department in a drowsy state following a 4-day history of intermittent moderate-grade fever without chills or rigors. On admission, her blood pressure is 96/66 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals impaired sensorium but no cutaneous rashes or active bleeding manifestations. Initial triage laboratory testing demonstrates severe thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 35,000/μL.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to acute febrile illness with altered sensorium and bilateral cerebral lesions; ruled out by neuroimaging demonstrating vasogenic edema without diffusion restriction, hemorrhage, or post-contrast enhancement, along with prompt and complete clinical and radiological resolution.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Based on the clinical and imaging findings, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and dengue encephalitis were considered as possible diagnoses.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the typical posterior reversible leukoencephalopathy pattern; however, classic hypertensive encephalopathy was excluded by the persistent absence of elevated blood pressure, with the patient instead presenting normotensive to hypotensive requiring dopamine for vascular tone.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There was no recorded hypertensive episode throughout the clinical course of the patient in our hospital.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was established by positive non-structural NS1 antigen testing in the setting of severe thrombocytopenia and characteristic vasogenic edema on neuroimaging that completely resolved on follow-up, confirming PRES secondary to dengue fever.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She tested positive for NS1 antigen and had a platelet count of 35 000/microl.
